newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: FATE OF SLOVAK REFERENDUMS IN DOUBT.
newsitem.headline: FATE OF SLOVAK REFERENDUMS IN DOUBT.

text.p: Weekend referendums whose outcome could decide whether Slovakia remains on course for Western integration have been muddled by a row over ballots tied to a years-long feud between the president and premier.

The twinned referendums, on Slovakia's desire for NATO membership and on whether the president should be directly elected, have been thrown into question as two separate versions of the ballots have begun being issued.
The referendum on direct presidential elections resulted from a petition drive by opposition parties.
It is seen as an attempt to prevent Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar from possibly assuming presidential powers when the term of incumbent Michal Kovac, an avowed foe of the premier, ends next March.

"The government fears the 'yes' vote in both referendums would be a defeat for its current policies and is doing all it can to thwart the plebiscite," Jan Budaj, secretary of the opposition Democratic Union told a news conference on Thursday.

The government led by Meciar -- who has clashed with President Michael Kovac since Kovac helped bring a previous Meciar government down in 1994 -- has made several attempts to delay or postpone the presidential referendum.

With the present composition of parliament, neither the ruling coalition nor the opposition would be able to muster the two-thirds majority to have their candidate elected, and the premier would assume presidential powers.
The Constitutional Court this week rejected two government motions to declare the presidential referendum illegal.
But then Meciar's interior minister Gustav Krajci on Wednesday ordered the distribution of ballots containing only the three questions on NATO membership.
"I take the responsibility for altering the ballot," Krajci said.

The Central Referendum Commission (UKR) responsible for overseeing the referendum, however, ruled that Krajci's move was illegal and that only ballots with all four questions and those with the official seal of the UKR were valid.

"If Krajci decides to distribute only ballots with the NATO questions without the presidential one, we will have no other alternative than to proclaim the entire referendum as invalid," Kalman Petocz an UKR member said.
Mayors from several districts told the private Radio Twist that state employees of district administrations had been ordered to distribute the interior-ministry ballots or face disciplinary measures.
"Somebody fears that we, the citizens will decide in Slovakia about the head of state," said an appeal issued on Thursday by the leaders of opposition parties.
The appeal calls on voters to register but reject ballot papers with only three questions and insist on ballots with all four propositions.
"We are carefully watching the way the referendums are being carried out, whether the authorities are guaranteeing a truly democratic poll," one western diplomat said.
"That is the yardstick of democratic maturity and will again be a test of whether Slovakia is ripe for integration into western structures," the diplomat added.
Meciar's government has also adopted a cool attitude to the NATO referendum questions despite official declarations of intent to join the alliance.

The ballot on NATO membership contains three questions: Are you in favour of Slovakia's membership in NATO? Are you in favour of the deployment of nuclear weapons on Slovak soil? Are you in favour of establishing military bases in Slovakia?

The alliance is to hold a summit in Madrid at the beginning of July at which it will invite some former east bloc countries to apply for NATO membership. The Czech Republic, Poland and Hungary are widely expected to be invited, while Slovakia, once considered a front-runner, no longer appears in the running.
Western diplomats have all but ruled out Slovakia's chances of being invited because of shortcomings in democratic reforms.
